newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major fights back on Europe as polls dip.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major fights back on Europe as polls dip.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, grabbing hold of his flagging election campaign, took the risky step of focussing on Europe again and accusing Labour leader Tony Blair of preparing to surrender Britain's interests.

Brandishing a draft review of European Union's treaties due to be hammered out at an Amsterdam summit in June, Major said Labour "may claim these days not to wave the red flag but they'd certainly go to Amsterdam and wave the white flag."

The Conservatives took out full-page adverts in national newspapers to drive home Major's opposition to a federal European state and his guarantee that Britain would not enter a single currency without a national referendum.

But Blair, whose drive to modernise the opposition Labour and ditch its old-style socialist dogma has given him a poll lead of 17 points or more, dismissed Major as the leader of a divided party at war with itself over Europe.
"You have got, two weeks out from a general election, a Conservative party in chaos, the leader having to appeal for unity," Blair told a news conference.
"If you vote Tory (Conservative) on May 1, what Conservative party are you going to get? Are you getting the Conservative party of Kenneth Clarke or the Conservative party of John Redwood?"
Chancellor of the Exchequer Clarke and anti-European former minister Redwood are at opposite ends of the spectrum of the European split in the Conseravtive Party.

Major has been left reeling by the decision of two junior ministers and more than 200 Conservative candidates to campaign against a single currency in defiance of government policy, which is to wait and see if it is in Britain's interest to join.

The civil war over Europe has been the issue which has dogged his attempts to unite the party throughout his six years as prime minister and forced him to stand down as party leader two years ago and challenge anti-European rebels to fight him.
Major won his risky gambit, but the splits were not healed and his defeated challenger, former cabinet member Redwood, piled on the pressure again on Thursday.

Redwood said Major had not "come across as strongly as some of us would like" on his plans for a single currency. Major said it was "frustrating" that some members of his party had acted "unwisely" by stepping out of line on a single currency.

But in a new concession to bring the so-called Euro-sceptics into line for the crucial 14 days remaining in the campaign that could end 18 years of Conservative rule, Major said he would not rule out allowing members of parliament a free vote when it came to deciding on the single currency.
Labour's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook immediately savaged Major for the concession, saying: "John Major has now abdicated all pretence at leadership of the Tory Party.

"Today he has admitted that he cannot command the support of his party and that he does not expect them to vote for government policy. The only initiative John Major took today was to throw in the towel."

Major's decision to take personal charge of the campaign, ditching prepared party television broadcasts to appear in person on Wednesday night to put his case on Europe, has overshadowed all other aspects of the campaign including good economic figures which the Conservatives hoped would boost their standing with voters.
Labour, while relishing their rivals' disarray, are also concerned that voters are not getting to hear the debate on key issues such as health and education.
